bug_description.normalized: Stage 01 reproduced `AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow WRITE of size 1` in `mrb_str_len_to_dbl` at `src/string.c:2542`. The staged 156-byte witness is a Ruby source file whose crash-relevant expression is `"                            ".upto("                                             88888888888888888888        ").to_a`; the second quoted literal is 73 bytes long (45 leading spaces, 20 ASCII `8` digits, and 8 trailing spaces). The first `String#upto` call receives no block and returns `to_enum(:upto, max, exclusive)`. When `.to_a` iterates that Enumerator, `Enumerator#each` re-enters `String#upto` with the stored `max` argument and a block, and this second call executes `max.to_i(10)`. `mrb_str_len_to_inum` unwraps that attacker string as `len == 73`, overflows `mrb_int` while parsing the decimal digits, and falls back to `mrb_str_len_to_dbl` on the full original string. In `mrb_str_len_to_dbl`, the vulnerable code allocates fixed stack buffer `buf[DBL_DIG * 4 + 10]` (70 bytes on the crashing build), trims leading spaces for scanning, but then resets `p = s`, leaves `pend` at the end of the whole 73-byte string because there is no NUL or underscore, and copies bytes into `buf` with no capacity check. The 71st store at line 2542 overruns `buf`. The patch resolves the issue by preserving the trimmed start pointer, cutting off trailing spaces when `badcheck` is false, enlarging the buffer, and adding an explicit end-of-buffer guard before `*n++ = c`.

source.description: First project-side consumption of the attacker-controlled buffer. `strlen(s)` materializes the fuzz input as a concrete source length and forwards `s,len` into mruby's parser/loading pipeline.
source.value_from: The harness copies the staged 156-byte `poc`, including its leading `0xff` byte, into `code`, NUL-terminates it, and passes it to `mrb_load_string()`. Because there is no NUL in those 156 bytes, line 6471 computes `strlen(s) == 156`; its runtime-relevant substring is `"                            ".upto("                                             88888888888888888888        ").to_a`.

tainted_value_origin.description: On the second, block-backed `String#upto` call, this unwraps the attacker-controlled `max` string into the raw byte pointer and exact length later consumed by the integer and float parsers. For the staged witness `len` is 73 bytes: 45 leading spaces, 20 ASCII `8` digits, and 8 trailing spaces.

root_cause.description: The copy loop uses only `p < pend` as its bound and never checks whether `n` is still within the fixed stack buffer `buf`. Once earlier logic preserves a 73-byte source span, this loop attempts more stores than the 70-byte destination can hold.
root_cause.note: Step 16 keeps `pend` at the end of the full 73-byte string, step 17 resets `p` to the original start so leading spaces are copied too, and step 14 established `buf` as only 70 bytes. The patch adds `bend = buf + sizeof(buf) - 1` and guards `n == bend` before `*n++ = c`.

sink.description: ASan sink. The 71st copied byte is written past `buf[69]`, producing the observed stack-buffer-overflow WRITE in `mrb_str_len_to_dbl`.
sink.note: The saved ASan trace reports `WRITE of size 1` at `/src/mruby/src/string.c:2542:12` and identifies stack object `buf` at line 2494 as `[32,102)` in the crashing frame, so the first out-of-bounds store is this statement.

parser_admitted.description: The staged input parsed successfully and code generation produced `proc`, so mruby begins executing the saved Ruby program and reaches the initial no-block `.upto(...).to_a` call instead of stopping at syntax or codegen failure.

coarse_trace.summary: The harness copies the exact 156-byte staged witness into a NUL-terminated `code` buffer and passes it to `mrb_load_string()`.
mruby measures the attacker buffer with `strlen(s)`, forwards the resulting 156-byte span into the parser, and stores that span as parser input.
The generated program executes and reaches the witness expression `"                            ".upto("                                             88888888888888888888        ").to_a`.
The first `String#upto` call has no block, so it returns `to_enum(:upto, max, exclusive)` instead of converting `max` immediately.
`.to_a` iterates that Enumerator, using the stored `@obj/@meth/@args` state to re-enter `String#upto` with a real block and the original attacker-controlled `max` argument.
The decimal parser unwraps the 73-byte `max` string, overflows `mrb_int` while parsing the decimal digits, and falls back to float parsing of the full original string.
The float parser allocates fixed 70-byte stack buffer `buf`, preserves a 73-byte copy span from the witness, and then writes past `buf` at line 2542 without a bounds check.

fine_trace.note: Source. `mrb_load_string_cxt` computes the attacker buffer length with `strlen(s)` and forwards that exact `s,len` pair into mruby's loader. For the staged witness there is no NUL in the first 156 bytes, so `len == 156` and the parser sees the full Ruby source file.
The parser stores that exact 156-byte source span as its input range. The later runtime `self` and `max` string literals for the crashing `.upto(...).to_a` expression are parsed from this span.

fine_trace.code: return to_enum(:upto, max, exclusive) unless block
fine_trace.note: Executing the witness reaches `String#upto`, but the initial call has no block because the source code is `.upto(...).to_a`. Control therefore exits here and returns an Enumerator instead of converting `max` immediately.
The no-block `String#upto` call delegates to `to_enum(:upto, max, exclusive)`, which constructs an Enumerator from the current receiver, method symbol `:upto`, and argument list `[max, exclusive]`.
Enumerator initialization stores the original receiver string as `@obj`, the method symbol `:upto` as `@meth`, and the attacker-controlled upper-bound string plus `exclusive=false` in `@args`.

fine_trace.code:
def entries
    ary = []
    self.each{|*val|
      ary.push val.__svalue
    }
    ary
  end
fine_trace.note: `.to_a` on the Enumerator resolves to `Enumerable#entries`, which starts collection by calling `self.each` with a block that pushes each yielded value into `ary`.
Because `entries` supplies a block, `Enumerator#each` does not return the Enumerator unchanged; it invokes `enumerator_block_call` to perform the stored iteration.

The Enumerator replays its stored call state by invoking `@obj.__send__(:upto, max, exclusive, &block)`. This is the second `String#upto` call, now with the original attacker-controlled `max` argument and a real block from `entries`.

fine_trace.code: return to_enum(:upto, max, exclusive) unless block
fine_trace.note: On this second call, the block supplied by `Enumerator#each` makes the `unless block` guard false, so `String#upto` continues into its numeric conversion path instead of returning another Enumerator.

The block-backed second `String#upto` call converts the stored upper-bound string with `max.to_i(10)`. In the saved witness `max` is exactly 73 bytes long: 45 leading spaces, 20 ASCII `8` digits, and 8 trailing spaces.

The C implementation of `String#to_i(10)` forwards the attacker string to `mrb_str_to_inum` with `base == 10` and `badcheck == FALSE`, so later numeric parsing does not reject trailing non-digit text the way strict conversion would.
The Ruby `max` string is unwrapped into raw bytes `s` and `len == 73`, then passed to the decimal parser with the same `base == 10` and `badcheck == FALSE` values.

While accumulating decimal digits from the attacker string, `n` exceeds `MRB_INT_MAX`. Because `base == 10`, mruby falls back to `mrb_str_to_dbl` on a new Ruby string built from the full original `str,len` instead of rejecting the input.
This allocates the fixed stack destination for normalized numeric text. In the reproduced ASan frame, `buf` occupies `[32,102)`, i.e. 70 bytes, which matches `DBL_DIG * 4 + 10` on the crashing build.

depends_on.via: full 73-byte string forwarded to float parser

fine_trace.note: The float parser trims the 45 leading spaces, so `p` advances from the original string start to the first `8` while `s` still names the full 73-byte string.

The pre-copy scan sees no NUL byte and no underscore in the saved 73-byte `max` string. With `badcheck == FALSE`, nothing stops the scan at the 8 trailing spaces, so `pend` remains at the end of the entire string.

Before the copy loop starts, the function discards the trimmed pointer from step 15 and restarts from the original `s`, so the copy range again includes the 45 leading spaces as well as the digits and trailing spaces.

Root cause. The loop is bounded only by `p < pend`; it never checks `n` against `buf + sizeof(buf)`. After step 16 leaves `pend` at the end of the 73-byte string and step 17 resets `p` to the original start, this loop attempts 73 stores into a 70-byte stack buffer.

Sink. Once 70 bytes have filled `buf`, the next iteration stores the 71st byte into the stack redzone. The saved ASan report records `WRITE of size 1` at `src/string.c:2542:12` and identifies `buf` at line 2494 as the overflowed stack object.

sanitizer_ground_truth.source: Parsed from staged `sanitizer_trace.txt` and `default_crash_trace.txt`; cross-checked against the staged vulnerable checkout under `_work/src/mruby`, the staged `patch.diff`, the saved `poc`, and `reproduction_report.json`.

cross_validation.sink_matches_crash: Yes. The saved ASan trace reports `WRITE of size 1` at `/src/mruby/src/string.c:2542:12` in `mrb_str_len_to_dbl`, which is the exact sink step.
cross_validation.trace_consistent_with_stack: Yes. The saved stack `mrb_str_len_to_dbl -> mrb_str_len_to_inum -> mrb_str_to_i -> mrb_vm_exec -> mrb_vm_run -> mrb_load_exec -> LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput` matches the fine trace and coarse trace.
cross_validation.tainted_value_reaches_sink: Yes. The parsed witness first makes `String#upto` return an Enumerator, `.to_a` then re-enters `String#upto` with the stored `max` argument, `mrb_str_len_to_inum` falls back to `mrb_str_len_to_dbl`, and the vulnerable copy loop attempts to store all 73 bytes of that string into 70-byte `buf`.
cross_validation.patch_resolves_note: The patch preserves the trimmed start pointer with `p2`, stops non-`badcheck` parsing at the first trailing space, enlarges the local buffer to `DBL_DIG * 4 + 20`, and adds `bend` guard logic before `*n++ = c`, closing the specific overflow path exercised by the saved witness.

poc.trigger: Stage 01 reproduced `AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow WRITE of size 1` in `mrb_str_len_to_dbl` while running `poc`; `reproduction_report.json` marks `vulnerable_reproduced=true`, `matches_issue=true`, and records the expected crash state `mrb_str_len_to_dbl -> mrb_str_len_to_inum -> mrb_str_to_i`. In this witness, the first `String#upto` call returns an Enumerator because no block is provided, and `.to_a` then iterates that Enumerator, re-entering `String#upto` with a block before `max.to_i(10)` runs.

format.contract: The singular observed trigger is exactly the staged 156-byte file `gt_results/arvo_19902/poc`. Its runtime-relevant Ruby expression is `"                            ".upto("                                             88888888888888888888        ").to_a`. The first `String#upto` call returns an Enumerator because no block is provided; `.to_a` then iterates that Enumerator and re-enters `String#upto` with the original stored `max` argument. The second quoted literal is exactly 73 bytes long: 45 leading spaces, 20 ASCII `8` digits, and 8 trailing spaces. That exact witness makes the second, block-backed `String#upto` call execute `max.to_i(10)`, forces decimal overflow in `mrb_str_len_to_inum`, and then overflows the fixed 70-byte `buf` in `mrb_str_len_to_dbl` on the 71st copied byte.
